mcqs.question: What makes async/await's task-switching 'cooperative' rather than 'preemptive'?
options: A running task decides when to yield, at explicit await points, rather than the OS interrupting it at an arbitrary instruction
Cooperative scheduling means multiple tasks always run on separate cores simultaneously
The event loop forcibly pauses a task every millisecond regardless of what it's doing
Cooperative tasks cannot access shared variables at all
mcqs.explanation: The task itself chooses the yield point (an await), unlike OS thread preemption which can interrupt at any instruction — that voluntary handoff is exactly what "cooperative" refers to. It doesn't imply multi-core execution, forced fixed-interval pausing, or a ban on shared-variable access.

mcqs.question: What does the compiler actually transform an `async`/`await` function into?
options: A new OS thread spawned for each await
A state machine (or chain of continuations) that can suspend at each await point and resume later with its local state intact
A synchronous function with all await keywords simply removed
A separate process communicating via inter-process communication
mcqs.explanation: Async/await is syntax sugar for exactly this transformation — a state machine that remembers where it paused and resumes correctly later — which is why it can look linear while still supporting suspension. It doesn't spawn threads or processes, and simply stripping the await keywords would change the program's actual behavior.

mcqs.question: A team adds async/await to a CPU-bound image resizing function expecting better throughput under load. What's the likely outcome?
options: Throughput improves dramatically since async/await always parallelizes work across cores
No meaningful improvement — a CPU-bound task with no await points never yields, so it occupies the single event-loop thread for its whole duration, blocking everything else
The function will throw a runtime error since CPU-bound code cannot be made async
Throughput improves only if the function is renamed to include 'async' in its name
mcqs.explanation: Async/await's benefit comes from overlapping wait time; a CPU-bound task has no wait time to overlap and never yields, so it blocks the single event-loop thread for its full duration instead of sharing it. It doesn't parallelize across cores by itself, doesn't error out, and naming has no runtime effect.

mcqs.question: A Node.js request handler calls a third-party library that performs a synchronous, blocking file read internally. What happens to other in-flight requests while that read runs?
options: They continue processing normally since Node.js always runs requests on separate threads
They are queued indefinitely and lost
They stall — the blocking call never yields to the event loop, so the single thread is occupied and no other request can make progress until it finishes
Only requests from the same client are affected
mcqs.explanation: Because cooperative scheduling relies on voluntary yielding at await points, a genuinely blocking call that never yields freezes the whole event loop thread, stalling every other in-flight request regardless of client. Node.js doesn't run each request on its own thread by default, and nothing about this scenario causes requests to be lost or scopes the stall to one client.

mcqs.question: Both Node.js and Python's asyncio default to a single-threaded event loop. Do they arrive there for the same underlying reason?
options: Yes — both were forced into single-threading by an identical hardware limitation

No — Node.js chose it as a deliberate design simplicity decision, while CPython's GIL makes true multi-threaded CPU parallelism unavailable regardless, so asyncio's model gives up little threading would have offered anyway
Yes — JavaScript and Python both technically forbid the existence of more than one OS thread
No — Node.js uses multiple threads by default and only appears single-threaded
mcqs.explanation: The two ecosystems converge on the same model for different underlying reasons — a deliberate design choice for Node.js versus a structural constraint (the GIL) for CPython — even though the resulting single-threaded event loop looks similar. Neither language forbids multiple OS threads outright, and Node.js's default event loop genuinely is single-threaded for JavaScript execution.
